1.pericope_label: And the men of Kirjath-jearim came, and fetched up the ark of the Lord, and brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill, and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep the ark of the Lord — and it came to pass, while the ark abode in Kirjath-jearim, that the time was long; for it was twenty years: and all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord

schools.summary: Say Kirjath-jearim, the home of the Ark for nearly fifty years, was probably selected as the nearest large city to Bethshemesh then in the hands of the Israelites. It was neither a priestly nor a Levitical city, but no doubt had preserved something of its ancient character of sanctity even among the children of Israel: in old days, before the Hebrew invasion, it was a notable high place and a seat of the worship of Baal, and this too was no doubt taken into account when it was resolved to locate the Ark there. The words in the hill remind us that the old high place was still marked, and was from its sacred associations looked on as a fitting temporary resting-place for the sacred treasure of Israel. On Eleazar, hold it most likely that Abinadab was a Levite, since the names Eleazar and Uzzah, and Ahio of the same family, are Levitical appellations; and Samuel, who though not named in this transaction was no doubt the director, would of course have endeavoured to find a man of the tribe of Levi for the sacred trust. Quote the description that this Eleazar was constituted not priest, but watchman at the grave of the Ark by its corpse, till the future joyful resurrection. Note that here the Ark remained until David brought it from the house on the hill, in the city of woods, first to the home of Obed-edom and then to his own royal Zion. On the note of time, render it, from the day that the Ark rested at Kirjath-jearim the time was long, for it was twenty years; and say there is something very touching in this sad note of time, so that we think we read Samuel’s own words here, the unwearied toiler for God and his people having found the twenty years a weary period of waiting. But do not suppose that the hungering of Israel after their God-Friend only began after the twenty years of sorrow were over: it had been a stern trial time, for the great victory of Aphek and the destruction of Shiloh had laid all Israel at the feet of their Philistine enemies, who made their supremacy bitterly felt, and the restoration of the Ark in no wise signified that they loosed their hold on the conquered people. This long time, when the hand of Philistia pressed so heavily, was the important period of Samuel’s life, in which he must have laboured incessantly to wake up the old worship of the Eternal and the pure life loved by God. The early dreams of his boy days, the hopes excited by his burning enthusiasm, were scattered to the winds; the fatal battle of Aphek, the capture of the holy Ark, the death of his old guardian the high priestly judge, the sack of the loved sanctuary and the continued oppression of Philistia had opened the eyes of the young inspired man of God. Taught by the bitter lessons of adversity, he saw it was by no bold stroke of a few gallant patriots that the nation could be saved, and that all such efforts, after the crushing defeat of Aphek, would only sink the nation into still lower depths of degradation and misery. Elsewhere run the two verses together and insist that they are not to be separated: the single clauses are connected by the consecutive particle, there is no gap between them, and they contain one closely and logically connected thought — there is no force at all in the proofs adduced by one scholar of a gap between them.

Say the men of Kirjath-jearim came and fetched up the ark from Bethshemesh, which was near them, and made no difficulty of fetching it but gladly received it; for if they knew of what happened to the men of Bethshemesh, they knew it was not owing to the presence of the ark among them, but to their irreverent behaviour toward it. And though Kirjath-jearim was not a Levite city, so that the men of it could not bear the ark themselves, they might have proper persons from Bethshemesh to do this service. On the length of the stay, say it could not be less than between forty and fifty years, for it remained here until the times of David, who removed it after he was made king over all Israel and had reigned over Judah seven years; and from the death of Eli to that time, which included the government of Samuel and of Saul, it could not be less than what has been hinted.

Attend the ark to Kirjath-jearim, and then leave it there, to hear not a word more of it, save once, till David fetched it thence about forty years after. We are very willing to attend it thither, for the men of Bethshemesh have by their own folly made that a burden which might have been a blessing, and gladly would we see it among those to whom it will be a savour of life unto life, for in every place where it has lately been it has been a savour of death unto death. Observe first that the men of Kirjath-jearim cheerfully bring it among them, coming at the first word; their neighbours were not more glad to be rid of it than these were to receive it, knowing very well that what slaughter the ark had made at Bethshemesh was not an act of arbitrary power but of necessary justice, and that those who suffered by it must blame themselves and not the ark — for we may depend upon the word which God hath said, provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt. Note that the judgments of God on those who profane his ordinances should not make us afraid of the ordinances, but of profaning them and making an ill use of them. Observe second that they carefully provided for its decent entertainment among them, as a welcome guest, with true affection, and as an honourable guest, with respect and reverence: they had no public building to adorn with it, but lodged it in the house of Abinadab, which stood upon the highest ground and probably was the best house in their city, or perhaps its master was the most eminent man they had for piety and best affected to the ark.

Give the chapter its argument first: the men of Kirjath-jearim bring the ark from Bethshemesh and consecrate Eleazar the son of Abinadab to keep it, and there it continues twenty years; Samuel reproves and exhorts the people and gathers them at Mizpeh, where they fast and pray and confess their sins; the Philistines go up against them, the Israelites cry to the Lord, Samuel offers sacrifice, and the Lord confounds the Philistines with thunder; Samuel erects a stone for a memorial and calls it Ebenezer; the Philistines are subdued and Israel recovers its lost cities; and Samuel acts as an itinerant judge in Israel. Then say that when these people received the message of the Bethshemites they probably consulted Samuel, with whom was the counsel of the Lord, and he encouraged them to go and bring it up, else they might have expected such destruction as happened to the Bethshemites; and that the sanctifying of Eleazar signifies no more than setting this man apart simply to take care of the ark. Elsewhere say the fetching up was by the priests appointed to that work; that this place was chosen both because it was strong, where the ark would be most safe, and because it was high and therefore visible at some distance, which was convenient for those who were at that time to direct their prayers and faces toward the ark — and for the same reason David afterwards placed it in the hill of Zion. Deny that they made Eleazar either Levite or priest, for in Israel persons were not made but born such; they devoted or set him apart wholly to attend upon this work, and chose him rather than his father because he was younger and stronger and probably freed from domestic cares which might divert or disturb him, his office being to keep the place where the ark was clean, and to guard it that none might touch it but such as God allowed. On the length of the stay, note that he does not say the twenty years were all the time of the ark’s abode there, for it continued from Eli’s time till David’s reign, which was forty years, but that it was so long there before the Israelites were sensible of their sin and misery; and say the ark was not carried back to Shiloh, its former place, either because that place was destroyed by the Philistines when the ark was taken, or because God would hereby punish the wickedness of the people by keeping it in a private place near the Philistines, whither the generality durst not come. Take the lamenting to mean that they followed after God with lamentations for his departure and prayers for his return.

debates: Why Kirjath-jearim was chosen for the ark.
Whether Eleazar was already a Levite or merely set apart.
How long the ark actually remained there.
Why the ark was never returned to Shiloh.
What Samuel was doing during the twenty silent years.
outliers: Ellicott suggests the town was chosen partly because it had been a Canaanite high place and seat of Baal worship.
Wesley denies that any man could be made a Levite or priest, since in Israel such persons were born and not made.
Ellicott holds the opposite, that Abinadab was probably already a Levite, on the evidence of family names.
Wesley reconciles the twenty years with the forty by making the twenty the time before Israel repented.
Ellicott reconstructs the twenty years as the formative period of Samuel’s life and hears his own voice in the note of time.
Ellicott quotes a description of Eleazar as watchman at the grave of the ark until its resurrection.
Keil and Delitzsch argue against a scholar who found a narrative gap between the two verses.

3.pericope_label: And Samuel spake unto all the house of Israel, saying, If ye do return unto the Lord with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the Lord, and serve him only — then the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the Lord only — and Samuel said, Gather all Israel to Mizpeh, and I will pray for you unto the Lord

schools.summary: Note that the strange gods are next described as Baalim, the plural form referring to the numerous images of Baal, as the plural Ashtaroth to those of the female goddess; both were favourite Phoenician deities, known under several familiar names, and they represented the productive power of nature, being generally worshipped throughout the East, usually with a wild and wanton worship. Then set out how dangerous the summons was. It was seemingly a desperate venture to which the prophet called unarmed and undisciplined Israel: they were completely at the mercy of their long victorious foes, who held the chief fortified places in the country with their garrisons, and Samuel challenged Israel to bid defiance to the most cherished institutions of their oppressors, bidding them, if they loved the Eternal, to turn aside from reverencing what Philistia held to be sacred and all-powerful. He knew well that what he urged would at once provoke what appeared a dangerous and most unequal contest; if defeated, Israel would bring on their devoted heads utter misery, and a ruin hitherto undreamed of even in their unhappy land. Had they courage and faith to plunge unarmed and undisciplined into so perilous a contest? For twenty years the great patriot-statesman had laboured for this end, and had succeeded at last in opening the eyes of Israel to the real cause of their misfortunes. When the answer came, say it showed how thoroughly the prophet-statesman had done his Master’s work: through the land the graven images of the Phoenician idols were thrown down and their impious worship boldly dishonoured, and once more, in bold defiance of the idol-worshipping Philistines, the Invisible and Eternal was throughout the land acknowledged as the one God — which was of course an open act of rebellion against that warlike people who for so long had ruled them with an iron rule. On the place, spell it Mizpah, a common name for lofty situations, signifying a watch-tower, a place where an outlook could be kept against an advancing enemy; and say the assembly of the tribes there marked a new departure for Israel, the result of more than twenty years of toil undertaken by the greatest reformer and statesman the chosen race ever knew. The gathering belonged both to religion and to war: its first object was solemnly to assure the Lord that the heart of his people, so long estranged, was again his; its second to implore that he might restore a repentant people to the land of their inheritance. What more likely than that the prophet-statesman, who at that juncture represented priest and judge and seer to Israel, devised on that momentous day new symbolic rites, signifying Israel’s new dedication for the future and repentance for the sad past? The solemn pouring out of water before the Lord symbolised, to a people trained so carefully to watch the meaning of symbols and imagery, the heart and whole inner life poured out before the Lord; the fasting represented the repentant humble sinner bowed down in grief before the one true God. Ask then whether it is not at least probable that the strange, mysterious custom we hear of in after days — the high priest filling the golden vessel with the waters of Siloam and then pouring it out silently before the Lord — was the record of one of the holiest memories of the people, their reconciliation with their God-Friend at Mizpeh. Elsewhere run the verses together and note that when Israel had turned to the Lord with all its heart and put away all its idols, Samuel gathered the people at Mizpeh to prepare them for fighting against the Philistines by a solemn day of penitence and prayer; for it is very evident that the object of calling all the people there was that the religious act performed might serve as a consecration for battle.

Say Samuel spake to all the house of Israel when they assembled at one of their three yearly feasts, or as he went from place to place, exhorting them to repentance and reformation, perceiving that they began to be awakened to a sense of their sins and seemed desirous of returning to God and restoring his worship. Note that they put away both their male and female deities. And fix the place: not Mizpeh in Gilead, on the other side of Jordan, but a city which lay on the borders of Judah and Benjamin, where the tribes had met before on the account of the Levite’s concubine; and say Samuel gave this order by messengers sent to the several tribes, or to the heads of them, to meet him there.

Wonder first where Samuel was and what he was doing all this while, for we have not had him so much as named for three chapters — not as if he were unconcerned, but his labours among his people are not mentioned till there appears the fruit of them. When he perceived that they began to lament after the Lord, he struck while the iron was hot, and endeavoured two things for them as a faithful servant of God and a faithful friend to the Israel of God. First, he endeavoured to separate between them and their idols, for there reformation must begin; he spoke to all the house of Israel, going, as it should seem, from place to place, an itinerant preacher, for we do not find that they were gathered together till later. Wherever he came this was his exhortation: if you do indeed return to the Lord, as you seem inclined to do by your lamentations for your departure from him and his from you, then know that you must renounce and abandon your idols, put away the strange gods, for your God will admit no rival — put them away from you, each one from himself, and put them from among you, doing what you can in your places to rid them out of the country. Note that Ashtaroth is particularly named because it was the best-beloved idol, and that which they were most wedded to; and note that true repentance strikes at the darling sin, and will with a peculiar zeal and resolution put away that, the sin which most easily besets us. On the assembly, say that Israel drew water and poured it out before the Lord, signifying their humiliation and sorrow for sin; they pour out their hearts in repentance before the Lord, and were free and full in their confession, and fixed in their resolution to cast away from them all their wrong doings. They made a public confession, We have sinned against the Lord, thus giving glory to God and taking shame to themselves — and if we thus confess our sins, we shall find our God faithful and just to forgive us.

Note that we have heard nothing of this judge since he served in the tabernacle, and that he was now grown up and established for a prophet in the land of Israel. Take the address to be to all the rulers and people too, as he had occasion in his circuit, mixing exhortation to repentance with his judicial administrations. Read the condition strictly: if you do indeed what you profess, if you are resolved to go on in what you seem to have begun; and with all your heart, that is sincerely and in good earnest, for outward services and professions will avail nothing. On the putting away, say, destroy their images, altars and groves, since they are strange and you do not know them as helpers, saviours or defenders; put them out of your houses, where some of you keep them, and out of your hearts, where they still have an interest in many of you; and especially Ashtaroth, whom they, together with the neighbouring nations, did more eminently worship. Take preparing the heart as letting it be straight and steady, purged from all sin and particularly from all inclinations to other gods; and serving him only as having no other religious service but his, and obeying his laws. Add that vain are your own exertions, for he will deliver you in such a way as to show that the excellence of the power is of himself alone. Note that Baalim and Ashtaroth were not two particular deities but two genera of idols, the one masculine and the other feminine, both words being in the plural number and signifying all their gods and goddesses. And on the gathering, say this appears to have been an armed assembly, though probably collected principally for religious and political purposes, since Samuel knew that an unarmed multitude could not safely be convened in the vicinity of the Philistines.

debates: Where Samuel had been during the twenty silent years.
Whether Baalim and Ashtaroth are two deities or two classes of idol.
Whether the assembly at Mizpeh was armed.
What the pouring out of water signified.
What the reform would cost politically.
outliers: Ellicott presents the reform as an act of open rebellion that invited an unequal war.
Ellicott suggests the later Temple rite of pouring the waters of Siloam commemorated this day at Mizpeh.
Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch independently make the gathering a consecration for battle.
Clarke argues the assembly must have been armed, since an unarmed crowd could not safely meet near the Philistines.
Henry explains Samuel’s long absence from the narrative by saying his labours are recorded only when their fruit appears.
Henry draws from the naming of Ashtaroth that true repentance strikes at the darling sin.
Clarke and Ellicott both treat the two names as plural classes rather than as individual gods.

6.pericope_label: And they gathered together to Mizpeh, and drew water, and poured it out before the Lord, and fasted on that day, and said there, We have sinned against the Lord: and Samuel judged the children of Israel in Mizpeh — and when the Philistines heard that the children of Israel were gathered together to Mizpeh, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel — and the children of Israel said to Samuel, Cease not to cry unto the Lord our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines

schools.summary: Call the drawing of water and pouring it out before the Lord a symbolical act, correctly explained on the whole by the Aramaic paraphrase, that they poured out their heart like water in penitence before the Lord. This is evident from the figurative expressions, poured out like water and pour out thy heart like water, which denote inward dissolution through pain, misery and distress; so that the pouring out of water before God was a symbolical representation of the temporal and spiritual distress they were then in, a practical confession before God: behold, we are before Thee like water that has been poured out. On the judging, note that for some quarter of a century Samuel had been the principal personage among the people and had long exercised the varied functions of the judges of Israel; but the tribes were scattered, their fortresses in the hand of enemies, and there was scarcely any national life in that gloomy period, so that in the first general assembly of the tribes the rank and position he had long really filled are publicly acknowledged. On the Philistine advance, say this was what might naturally have been expected: the sudden destruction of the Phoenician idol shrines throughout the country, followed immediately by the summons of a vast popular assembly held in so conspicuous a place, aroused at once the warlike nation which had so long kept Israel in servitude, and the Philistine leaders promptly assemble a powerful force and proceed to interrupt the gathering. On the appeal, say the fear was very natural: unarmed, or at least very poorly armed and equipped, the assembled Israelites saw from the heights the advancing Philistine army, and what hope was there for their ill-disciplined masses when they joined battle with that trained host of fighting men? But they remembered the days of old, and how, when Moses prayed, the Angel of his presence saved them; had they not with them there a seer equal to Moses, greater than Joshua, one with whom the Eternal of Hosts was wont to speak as friend speaketh with friend? So in that supreme hour of danger they turned to Samuel the seer. And Samuel, hurriedly — for the time was short and the foe close at hand — and with rites somewhat different from those enjoined in the Law, for the occasion was indeed a critical one, offered up a sacrifice and raised that weird piercing cry which many in Israel had heard before when Samuel prayed; and while the prophet-statesman was sustaining that loud imploring cry, while the smoke of the slain lamb was still ascending, the first line of the Philistine army appeared on the topmost slope of Mizpeh. Once more, as in old days, the glorious Arm fought with no earthly weapons for the people: an awful thunderstorm burst over the combatant hosts, the storm probably beating in the faces of the advancing Philistines, and the tribes welcomed it as the answer to their prophet’s prayer and charged down and broke their serried ranks. Elsewhere run the verses through and note that when the Philistines advanced during the offering of the sacrifice, the Lord thundered with a great noise against them, and threw them into confusion, so that they were smitten before Israel.

Say they gathered together to Mizpeh, even all Israel, at least the heads of the people and their representatives. Note that the Philistines heard of it, not knowing it was upon a religious account, but supposing they met to form schemes and measures to cast off their yoke and deliver themselves, and were preparing to take up arms and fall upon them. And note that the children of Israel applied to Samuel, not as the general of their forces but as the prophet of the Lord, believing his prayers for them would be of more avail than an army of men ever so numerous or so well accoutred.

Observe that the Philistines invade Israel, taking umbrage from that general meeting for repentance and prayer as if it had been a rendezvous for war, and, if so, thinking it prudent to keep the war out of their own country. They had no just cause for this suspicion; but those that seek to do mischief to others will be forward to imagine that others design mischief to them. See here first how evil sometimes seems to come out of good: the religious meeting of the Israelites at Mizpeh brought trouble upon them from the Philistines, which perhaps tempted them to wish they had stayed at home and to blame Samuel for calling them together. We may be in God’s way and yet meet with distress; nay, when sinners begin to repent and reform, they must expect that Satan will muster all his force against them, and set his instruments on work to the utmost to oppose and discourage them. But see second how good is, at length, brought out of that evil. Israel could never be threatened more seasonably than at this time, when they were repenting and praying, nor could they have been better prepared to receive the enemy; nor could the Philistines have acted more impolitely for themselves than to make war upon Israel at this time, when they were making their peace with God. But God permitted them to do it, that he might have an opportunity immediately of crowning his people’s reformation with tokens of his favour, and of confirming the words of his messenger, who had assured them that if they repented God would deliver them out of the hand of the Philistines. Thus he makes man’s wrath to praise him.

Admit that it is not easy to know what is meant by the drawing and pouring out of water. Pouring out water in the way of libation was a religious ordinance among the Hebrews, and among most other nations, particularly the Greeks and Romans, who used not only water but wine, milk, honey and blood, as we find by the poets and philosophers — and our Lord seems to allude to the ceremony. But the Aramaic paraphrast understands the place differently, translating that they poured out their hearts in penitence, as waters, before the Lord; and that deep penitential sorrow was represented under the notion of pouring out water we have direct proof in the psalmist, who says, I am poured out like water, my heart is like wax, it is melted in the midst of my bowels; and the prophet exhorts fallen Jerusalem under the same similitude to pour out her heart like water before the face of the Lord; and the psalmist uses the same image again in bidding the people pour out their hearts before him; and so does Hannah, who was a woman of a sorrowful spirit and poured out her soul before the Lord. Perhaps therefore the drawing and pouring out of water was done emblematically, to represent the contrition of their hearts. Or take it as an external sign whereby they testified both their own filthiness and need of washing by the grace and Spirit of God and the blood of the covenant, and their sincere desire to pour out their hearts before the Lord in true repentance, and to cleanse themselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit; and gloss before the Lord as in the public assembly, where God is in a special manner present. On the judging, say he gave them ordinances, heard and redressed grievances, and taught them how to get reconciled to God, so that the assembly was held for religious, political and military purposes at once; or that he governed them, reformed all abuses against God or man, took care that the laws of God should be observed and wilful transgressions punished. On the Philistine advance, say they went to give battle before Israel should become too powerful by continual accessions of numbers, and that Israel was afraid, being a company of unarmed persons and unfit for battle. And on the appeal, put it in their mouths: we are afraid to look God in the face because of our great wickedness, do thou therefore intercede for us as Moses did for his generation. They had reason to expect this, because he had promised to pray for them and had promised them deliverance, and they had been observant of him in all that he had spoken to them from the Lord. Thus they who receive Christ as their lawgiver and judge need not doubt of their interest in his intercession; and what a comfort is it to all believers that he never ceaseth, but always appears in the presence of God for us.

debates: What the pouring out of water signified.
Whether the assembly was religious, political or military.
Whether the Philistines had reason to read the gathering as a muster.
Why Israel appealed to Samuel rather than armed themselves.
By what rites Samuel offered the sacrifice.
outliers: Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch both adopt the Aramaic reading of the water as the heart poured out in penitence.
Wesley alone adds a second sense, of washing and cleansing, to the pouring out.
Clarke calls the assembly religious, political and military at once.
Henry observes that those who plan mischief are quick to suspect it in others.
Henry draws a double moral, that evil seemed to come of good and good was at length brought out of that evil.
Ellicott concedes that Samuel sacrificed with rites somewhat different from those enjoined in the Law.
Wesley reads the request for intercession as the type of Christ’s unceasing intercession.

9.pericope_label: And Samuel took a sucking lamb, and offered it for a burnt offering wholly unto the Lord: and Samuel cried unto the Lord for Israel; and the Lord heard him — and the Lord thundered with a great thunder on that day upon the Philistines, and discomfited them — then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Eben-ezer, saying, Hitherto hath the Lord helped us — so the Philistines were subdued, and they came no more into the coast of Israel

schools.summary: Note that when the Philistines advanced during the offering of the sacrifice, the Lord thundered with a great noise against them, that is with loud peals, and threw them into confusion, so that they were smitten before Israel. On the pursuit, say that as soon as they took to flight the Israelites advanced from Mizpeh and pursued and smote them to below Beth-car, whose situation, mentioned only here, has not yet been discovered; note the form given it by Josephus, and gloss the name as house of the lamb, or as some would render it house of the field, supposing it a Philistine fortress where the scattered remains of the beaten host were able to rally and defend themselves. On the memorial, say Samuel placed a stone between Mizpeh and Shen and gave it the name stone of help, as a standing memorial that the Lord had thus far helped his people; the situation of Shen is also unknown, but the name, meaning tooth, seems to indicate a projecting point of rock, or a place situated on such a point — answering to the modern French word for a tooth, a favourite name for a peak in some districts of the Alps and Pyrenees. On the subjugation, say that through this victory obtained by the miraculous help of God the Philistines were so humbled that they no more invaded the territory of Israel with lasting success as they had done before; this limitation of the words is implied in the context, for the words which immediately follow, that the hand of the Lord was against them all the days of Samuel, show that they made attempts to recover their lost supremacy but were unable to effect anything so long as Samuel lived. The defeats inflicted on them by Saul also belong to the days of Samuel, who died but a very few years before Saul himself. Then take the wider view: the work of Samuel had been thorough, and this was no mere solitary victory but the sign of a new spirit in Israel, which animated the nation during his lifetime and the reigns of the great Hebrew kings. The petty jealousies had disappeared and given place to a great national desire for unity: in the several tribal districts it was no longer the glory and prosperity of Judah, Ephraim or Benjamin, but the glory and prosperity of Israel that was aimed at. The old idol worship of Canaan, which corrupted and degraded every nationality which practised it, was in great measure swept away, while the pure religion of the Eternal was no longer confided solely to the care of the tribe of Levi, which had shown itself unworthy of the mighty trust. The Levites still ministered in the sanctuary, and when the Temple took its place alone officiated in its courts, and the chosen race of Aaron alone wore the jewels and the official robe of the high priest; but in religious matters the power of the priestly tribe was never again supreme in the Land of Promise. From the days of Samuel a new order — that of the Prophets, whose exact functions with regard to the ritual were undefined — was acknowledged by the people as the regular medium of communication.

Note that the lamb might be a sucking lamb and yet more than eight days old, for under that it might not be sacrificed. On the offering, say he might do it by a priest, as one Jewish commentator suggests, he being only a Levite; though, being a prophet and an extraordinary person, and this an extraordinary case, he might do it himself, as Gideon and others did, as well as offer it in another place than where the tabernacle was — Shiloh being now destroyed, persons and places for sacrifice were dispensed with. Say the men of Israel went out of Mizpeh, encouraged by hearing or perceiving that the army of the Philistines was discomfited by the thunder and lightning. Say Samuel took a stone and set it, not for worship, but as a monument of the victory obtained by the help of God. And on the subduing, say not that their country was conquered, or that they were made subject and become tributaries to Israel, but that they were so humbled as not to attempt to give the people of Israel any further trouble and distress, who were now delivered from their oppression and tyranny.

Give a short account of the further good services Samuel did to Israel: having parted them from their idols and brought them home to their God, he had put them into a capacity of receiving further benefits by his ministry, and having prevailed in that, he becomes in other instances a great blessing to them — yet, writing it himself, he is brief in the relation. We are not told here, but it appears elsewhere, that in the days of Samuel the prophet the people kept the ordinance of the passover with more than ordinary devotion, notwithstanding the distance of the ark and the desolations of Shiloh. Many good offices, no doubt, he did for Israel, but here we are only told how instrumental he was, first, in securing the public peace: in his days the Philistines came no more into the coast of Israel, made no inroads or incursions upon them, for they perceived that God now fought for Israel and that his hand was against the Philistines, and this kept them in awe and restrained the remainder of their wrath. Samuel was a protector and deliverer to Israel, not by dint of sword, as Gideon, nor by strength of arm, as Samson, but by the power of prayer to God and carrying on a work of reformation among the people; and religion and piety are the best securities of a nation. And second, in recovering the public rights: by his influence Israel had the courage to demand the cities which the Philistines had unjustly taken from them and long detained.

Note that this sucking lamb must have been eight days under its mother before it could be offered, as the law says. Then meet the difficulty: though Samuel was not a priest, yet he offered this sacrifice; or he might have ordered Eleazar to offer it and still be said to have done it himself, for he who procures a thing to be done may be said to do it himself. His not sacrificing at the tabernacle was justified by the necessity of the case, since neither tabernacle nor ark was at hand. Say he cried unto the Lord, making intercession with the sacrifice — so Christ intercedes in virtue of his satisfaction, and in all our prayers we must have an eye to his great oblation, depending on him for audience and acceptance. Render the thunder literally, the Lord thundered with a great voice, and say he confounded them with a mighty tempest of thunder and lightning, and no doubt slew many by the lightning. Of Beth-car say we know not where the place was, and give the forms found in the Greek, the Aramaic, the Syriac and the Arabic. On the stone, call it a rude unpolished stone, which was not prohibited by the law against images, there being no danger of worshipping such a stone, and this being set up only as a monument of the victory; name it the stone of help, and note that this victory was gained in the very same place where the Israelites had received their former fatal loss. Press the word hitherto: he hath begun to help us, though not completely to deliver us — by which wary expression he exciteth both their thankfulness for mercy received and their holy fear and care to please and serve the Lord, that he might help and deliver them effectually. And on the subduing, say a more signal victory was perhaps never gained by Israel, for the Lord had brought them low, almost to extermination, and now by his miraculous interference lifts them completely up and humbles their proud oppressors to the dust; God often suffers nations and individuals to be brought to the lowest extremity, that he may show his mercy and goodness by suddenly rescuing them when all human help has most evidently failed. But limit the words: they came no more with a great host, but only with straggling parties or garrisons; and all the days of Samuel means all the days while Samuel was their sole judge or ruler, for in Saul’s time they did come.

debates: How Samuel, who was not a priest, could lawfully offer the sacrifice.
Where Beth-car and Shen were.
In what sense the Philistines came no more.
What the word hitherto concedes.
What the victory changed in Israel besides the military situation.
outliers: Clarke allows that Samuel may have offered by proxy, and pleads necessity for the irregular place.
Gill prefers to make the irregularity a prophet’s extraordinary licence, as with Gideon.
Ellicott identifies Shen with the French dent, a name given to peaks in the Alps and Pyrenees.
Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley independently limit came no more from the very next clause of the verse.
Wesley presses hitherto as a guarded word, conceding that the deliverance was begun and not complete.
Ellicott argues that from this day the priestly tribe was never again supreme, the prophets taking its place.
Henry contrasts Samuel with Gideon and Samson: he delivered by prayer and reformation, not by the sword.

14.pericope_label: And the cities which the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron even unto Gath — and there was peace between Israel and the Amorites — and Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life — and he went from year to year in circuit to Bethel, and Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places — and his return was to Ramah; for there was his house; and there he built an altar unto the Lord

schools.summary: Say that in consequence of the defeat the Philistines were obliged to restore the cities they had taken, from Ekron to Gath; and take this definition of the limits as exclusive, signifying that the Israelites received back their cities up to the very borders of the Philistines, measuring those borders from Ekron to Gath, and not that they received Ekron and Gath also. For although these chief cities had been allotted to Judah and Dan in the time of Joshua, and although Judah and Simeon conquered Ekron with Gaza and Askelon after his death, the Israelites did not obtain any permanent possession. Or say it is doubtful whether the words signify that at this period these famous Philistine cities fell into Samuel’s hands, the expression more probably indicating on the Philistine side the direction and limits of the space in which Israel recovered its lost territory. Note that the immediate result of the victory, and of the renovated national spirit, was the recovery of the towns and villages which had fallen into Philistine hands. On the Amorites, say they are especially mentioned as representing the most powerful of the old Canaanite tribes, and that this note tells us that in these glorious days of restoration not only were the Philistines of the coast kept in check and gradually subdued, but the Canaanite tribes of the interior submitted quietly to the old conditions imposed at the conquest. On the judgeship, say that with the calling of the people to Mizpeh and the victory obtained through his prayer Samuel had assumed the government of the whole nation, so that his office as judge dates from that period, although he had laboured as prophet since the death of Eli and had thereby prepared the way for the conversion of Israel; and that its duration was all the days of his life, as his activity during Saul’s reign and the anointing of David sufficiently prove. Or say that his influence and supreme power only ended with his life; that for a very long period, probably at least twenty years after the decisive battle, he exercised the chief authority as judge; that the time at length arrived when, convinced by clear divine monition that it was best for the people that a king should rule over them, Samuel, then advanced in years, voluntarily laid down his high office in favour of the new king; but that his influence remained, and his authority, whenever he chose to exercise it, seems to have continued undiminished, king and nation submitting to his counsel on momentous occasions. On the circuit, observe that these centres were all situated in the southern part of the land, in the tribe of Benjamin, which leads to the conclusion that the power of Samuel, if not exclusively, was chiefly exercised among the southern tribes. The whole subsequent story of the chosen people seems to tell us that the religion of the Eternal at an early date became corrupted in the north of the Promised Land, and that the restoration of faith and purification of life which resulted from Samuel’s great work was so much less marked in the northern than in the southern tribes, that when the strong hand of Solomon was removed a formal secession from the southern league at once took place, followed by a rapid deterioration both in faith and practice in the northern kingdom. Add that the places named as centres were all holy sites, and at different periods of the year were no doubt crowded with pilgrims from distant parts. On Ramah, say it is the same Ramah of the Watchers where his parents had dwelt, and that after the destruction of Shiloh Samuel seems to have fixed his abode in his father’s city; and that in building an altar he followed the old custom of the patriarchs. It must be remembered that at this period there was no national sanctuary, no formal seat of worship where the high priest and his attendant priests and Levites served: the Ark was in safe keeping at Kirjath-jearim, but in private custody, and we hear of no priests and Levites, of no ritual or religious observances, in connection with its long sojourn there. It is probable that the sacred vessels and furniture had been saved from the destruction of Shiloh by Samuel, and were very likely in the prophet-judge’s keeping at Ramah.

Note that we nowhere read that the Israelites went out to war with the Philistines and took these cities from them by besieging and assaulting them; but they made a demand of them after the victory, by which the Philistines were so intimidated that they quietly surrendered them. On the judgeship, say he judged Israel not only before Saul was made king but afterwards; for though he had not the exercise of the supreme government, he might act as a judge under Saul, hear and try causes brought before him, and execute justice and judgment, and as a prophet teach and instruct the people and reform abuses among them; besides, he held and exercised the extraordinary office to which he was raised up of God, and even took upon him to reprove Saul himself. The Jews say he judged Israel thirteen years only, eleven by himself and two with Saul, but his government must have been much larger. On the circuit, render it from the year in the year, that is from the time of the year in the year, or as one paraphrase has it from the middle of it, that is every half year — and note that Josephus says he went twice a year in circuit. And on the return, say that when he had gone his circuit he came back to this city, which was his native place, and where his father and mother had dwelt.

Say we are not informed of the particulars of these reprisals, but we may rest assured all this was not done in one day: perhaps the retaking of the cities was by slow degrees, through the space of several years. Take the peace to be an agreement for the cessation of all acts of hostility, and the Amorites to be the Canaanites, often so called because these were formerly the most valiant of all those nations and the first enemies the Israelites met when they went to take possession of their land; say they made this peace with the Canaanites that they might be more at leisure to oppose the Philistines, now their most potent enemies, and that all the remaining Canaanites kept quiet and did not attempt to molest Israel when they found the Philistines, the most powerful of the ancient inhabitants, broken and subdued. On the judgeship, do the arithmetic: Samuel is supposed to have lived a hundred years, and did not begin to judge till he was about forty, so that he must have been a judge sixty years and consequently filled the office during the whole of Saul’s reign — though it is evident from the transactions with the witch of Endor that he had died before Saul’s last battle, and probably not long before. Samuel was the prophet of that time, declared the will of the Lord, and frequently directed both the civil and military transactions of the kingdom; and he seems, in many respects, to have been considered the governor of the people, while Saul was only looked on as the general of the armies. Or say that though Saul was king in Samuel’s last days, Samuel did not cease to be a judge, being so made by God’s extraordinary call, which Saul could not destroy, and therefore did sometimes, upon great occasions though not ordinarily, exercise the office of judge after the beginning of Saul’s reign. On the circuit, place the towns: when he was at Bethel, the tribe of Ephraim and all the northern parts of the country could attend him; when at Gilgal, the tribe of Benjamin and those beyond Jordan might have easy access to him; and when at Mizpeh, he was within reach of Judah, Simeon and Gad — but Ramah was the place of his ordinary abode, and there he held his court. Say he went to these several places in compliance with the people, whose convenience he was willing to purchase with his own trouble, as an itinerant judge and preacher, and that by his presence in several parts he could the better observe and rectify all sorts of miscarriages. And on the altar, say that being duly consecrated, the worship performed at it was strictly legal; that Ramah was the seat of prophecy during his life, and that thither all Israel probably came to consult him on matters of a spiritual nature, as there was the only altar of God in the land. Add that he built it that by joining sacrifices with his prayers he might the better obtain direction and assistance from God upon all emergencies; that this was done by prophetical inspiration, as appears by God’s acceptance of the sacrifices offered on it; and that indeed, Shiloh being now laid waste and no other place yet appointed, the law which obliged them to one place was for the present suspended, so that, as the patriarchs did, he built an altar where he lived, and that not only for the use of his own family but for the good of the country who resorted to it.

debates: Whether Ekron and Gath themselves were recovered.
How Samuel could judge all his life if Saul was king.
Whether Samuel’s authority extended to the northern tribes.
How an altar at Ramah could be lawful.
How the cities came back without a recorded campaign.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott independently read the boundary phrase as exclusive of the two cities named.
Clarke calls Samuel the governor of the people and Saul merely the general of the armies.
Wesley makes the judgeship indestructible, given by a call the king could not annul.
Clarke spreads the three circuit towns over the whole nation; Ellicott notes they all lie in the south and infers a southern ministry.
Ellicott builds the later secession of the northern kingdom on that same observation.
Ellicott conjectures that Samuel saved the sacred vessels from Shiloh and kept them at Ramah.
Gill notes that no campaign is recorded, the cities being surrendered to a demand.
